overview: German South West Africa was a colony imposed on existing African societies in the territory now called Namibia. German rule lasted from 1884 to 1915. Settler expansion, African resistance, genocide and forced labour shaped this period; the map’s 1914 to 1920 interval captures only its late aftermath.

periods.title: Colonial expansion
periods.summary: Treaties, settlement and military pressure extended German power over existing African communities.

periods.title: War and genocide
periods.summary: German forces committed genocide against Herero and Nama communities during the colonial war.

periods.title: After German defeat
periods.summary: South African forces defeated the German colonial government in 1915; the imported label persists beyond that ending.

items.text: Nama, Oorlam and Herero communities already had their own political relationships before German rule. Herero cattle wealth and expanding trade were central to nineteenth-century changes. Colonial “protection” treaties entered this existing world; they did not create a society on empty land.

Windhoek became the seat of German colonial administration in 1891. Colonial authorities divided the town into white and Black residential areas. Where a family could live became part of racial government, as consequential in daily life as decisions made in official offices.

A metal pass marker from Swakopmund, dated 1907, survives in a German museum exhibition. It bears a crown, place-name and identifying number. The portable metal object made colonial classification tangible, reducing an individual to an official number.

In the war beginning in 1904, German troops forced Herero survivors into the waterless Omaheke after the battle at Waterberg. Nama communities also resisted. Mass killing, deadly confinement and deprivation formed a genocide whose consequences continue in families and communities today.

Hendrik Witbooi’s letter journals preserve an African leader reasoning about colonial power and trying to build cooperation against it. UNESCO recognizes these documents for their political and literary importance. His community’s ideas survive in its own correspondence, alongside the records made by colonizers.

In a letter dated 13 October 1885, Witbooi told Maharero that he was short of supplies, including coffee and tobacco, and asked for them along his route. Diplomatic journeys required provisions. Even a political letter could include what amounted to a shopping request.

The same letter ends “Ik ben Uwen Vriend”, meaning “I am your friend”. This is a short example of Witbooi’s historical Dutch correspondence, preserved here through a 1929 printed transcription. Dutch writing was one medium for communication between African leaders in this multilingual region.

An incoming 1892 letter from Samuel Maharero discusses where people should settle near rivers and fears that outsiders would take the land. It closes with greetings to Witbooi’s wife and children. Diplomacy, family relationships and the practical question of where to live belonged in the same correspondence.

Nakambale Museum’s photographic exhibition includes images made by Finnish missionaries, the oldest from 1893. One shows King Kambonde, his wife and a missionary’s wife. Such photographs preserve clothing and encounters, while their framing reflects the people who operated the camera.

Railways changed the movement of goods across the colony, but tracks did not build themselves. A Namibian museum review draws attention to African labourers, including prisoners forced to work during the 1904 to 1908 war, whom older displays centered on German engineers largely omitted.

During the 1915 South African campaign, Black workers repaired damaged tracks, extended railway connections and unloaded supplies. Surviving photographs show these tasks. Moving water, food and ammunition made military movement possible, although the workers often receive less attention than commanders.

The German surrender document was signed on 9 July 1915 and reproduced in a contemporary campaign account. It records a military and governmental defeat. It did not restore independent government to the African communities whose land had been colonized.

ending.text: German colonial rule ended with surrender to South African forces in July 1915. South African administration followed, rather than immediate Namibian independence. Herero, Nama and other communities survived dispossession and genocide, maintaining families, political claims and remembrance beyond the colonial regime.
